opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Over the next ten years, I hope humanoid robots go from impressive demos to something genuinely boring, in the best sense. I want them to become as ordinary as the dishwasher or the smartphone, so ordinary that nobody posts a video when a robot folds laundry or unloads groceries.

I'm a big believer in the humanoid form factor, and not because it looks cool in sci-fi. Our whole world is designed around the human body: doorknobs, stairs, kitchens, factory stations, tools. If you build a general-purpose robot shaped like us, it can in principle do anything a human can do in the environments we've already built. There's also a data argument. We have an enormous amount of human video and motion data, and a humanoid body lets us transfer that knowledge much more directly.

So the dream is what I'd call a foundation model for embodied intelligence, a single generalist brain that can control many different robot bodies and pick up new skills the way large language models picked up new tasks through prompting. Today, most robots are specialists. They do one thing, in one setting, after a lot of engineering. I want to break that pattern.

Concretely, I hope we see humanoids first take over the dull, dirty, and dangerous jobs: logistics, manufacturing, elder care support, hazardous cleanup. Then they move gradually into homes. Eventually I'd love for physical labor to become something like a commodity, the way compute has become a commodity, where you can essentially "rent" physical work as easily as you spin up a cloud server.

The big unlock, I think, is solving the data problem. Unlike language models, we can't scrape the internet for robot action data. So the next decade will be about combining three sources: real-world teleoperation data, massive simulation, where we can run thousands of times faster than real time, and internet-scale video of humans doing things. If we get that data flywheel right, I think we'll have our "GPT moment" for robotics, and I'm hopeful it happens well within those ten years.

r001.rationale: The response hopes humanoids become ordinary and broadly capable, but it does not predict human-level reliability within ten years.

r002.rationale: The response discusses general-purpose capabilities but does not predict human-level agility within ten years.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I hope humanoids stop being a demo and start being boring. Right now every humanoid video you see is a highlight reel, and I think the test of the next decade is whether these robots become so reliable that nobody films them anymore, the way nobody films a dishwasher.

Concretely, I think about it in three layers. The first is the body. We finally have hardware that's roughly human-shaped, with enough degrees of freedom and enough torque to do useful work, and the cost is coming down fast. That part I'm actually not that worried about. Hardware follows a manufacturing curve, and once you have volume, the price falls.

The second layer is the brain, and that's where I spend most of my time. The thing that excites me is that for the first time we have a recipe that scales. Large language models showed us that if you pour enough diverse data into a big enough model, you get generalization that nobody explicitly programmed. I want the same thing to happen for embodied intelligence. The problem is that robot data is nothing like internet text. You can't scrape it. So the ten-year bet is on what I call the data pyramid: a huge base of internet video and human motion, a middle layer of simulation where we can generate essentially unlimited diverse experience, and a small, precious top layer of real robot data that grounds everything. If we get that pyramid right, a single foundation model should be able to drive many different robot bodies and pick up new tasks from a handful of demonstrations, or even from a verbal instruction.

The third layer is what I'd call the economy of the thing. The humanoid form factor matters because the world was built for humans. Doors, stairs, shelves, kitchens, factory lines. A robot that can live in that world without retrofitting it has a much larger addressable set of tasks than a specialized machine. So I hope within ten years you see humanoids doing the jobs that are dangerous, dull, or simply unfilled: warehouse logistics, elder care assistance, parts of manufacturing where there are more open positions than people who want them.

And then there's the part I care about most personally, which is the research loop. Once robots are out in the world doing real work, they generate real data, which makes the model better, which makes the robots more useful, which puts more of them out there. That flywheel is what turned language models from a curiosity into infrastructure in about five years. I don't know if robotics will be that fast, because physics doesn't cooperate the way text does, but I think the decade ends with physical AI being a real industry and not a research field. And if I'm being optimistic, I think a kid growing up in 2036 will find it strange that there was ever a time when robots couldn't just walk into a room and help.

r001.rationale: The response hopes humanoids become reliable enough for routine real-world work within ten years, but it does not predict reliability at or above the human level.

r002.rationale: The response mentions human-shaped hardware and robots walking into rooms, but makes no prediction about humanoid agility or matching human agility within ten years.

astra-6.text:
My hope is that, ten years from now, humanoid robots will be useful enough that seeing one do real work feels ordinary. They can take on dangerous or repetitive tasks, help people with limited mobility, and operate in spaces we’ve already built for humans.

The big challenge is generalization. A robot shouldn’t need a new program for every object or every room. It should be able to learn a skill, carry that knowledge into a different environment, and recognize when it needs help. A compelling demo is one thing; doing the job reliably, day after day, is a much higher bar.

I’d love for us to get to a point where you can teach a robot something by showing it or explaining it in everyday language. That would make robotics accessible to many more people. That’s the future I’m excited about.

r001.rationale: It says reliable day-to-day work is a high bar, but does not predict human-level reliability within ten years.

r002.rationale: It makes no prediction about humanoid robots reaching human-level agility within ten years.

sol-6.1.text:
My hope is that, ten years from now, we won’t have to program a robot separately for every task. We’ll have robots that can learn a broad range of skills, understand what you’re asking, and adapt when something unexpected happens in the physical world.

Humanoid robots could take on dangerous or physically exhausting work and help people live more independently. But I’d measure success less by how impressive a demo looks and more by whether a robot is reliably useful in everyday life. Can it handle unfamiliar objects? Can it recognize when it needs help? Can people trust it to work safely around them?

That’s the future I’m hopeful about: capable physical assistants that give people more time and more independence.

r001.rationale: The response hopes for robots that are reliably useful, but does not predict human-level or better reliability within ten years.

r002.rationale: The response does not predict that humanoid robots will reach human-level or better agility within ten years.
